headline: US markets nudged higher last night while the ASX had a quiet session today — all eyes on RBA rate expectations and GTA 6 pre-orders as the week's big themes.

portfolio.summary: A fairly calm day across the portfolio. The biggest moves came from your US holdings last night — Take-Two slid nearly 2.5% while Alphabet nudged up. On the ASX, everything barely moved, which is fine given the broader market uncertainty around rates and oil.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Dropped $5.29 last night to $222.26 USD. No single smoking-gun news item, but there's noise around Take-Two shutting down GTA Online RP servers ahead of GTA 6's launch — possibly unsettling some investors who worry about community backlash before the big release.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Slipped about $4 last night to $414.55 USD. No major breaking news — likely some profit-taking after a strong run. AI revenue growth remains a talking point but analysts are starting to scrutinise whether that revenue justifies the stock's valuation.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Up nearly 1% last night to $386.60 USD. Google launched 'Gemini Omni' today — a new all-in-one AI model — which is keeping positive sentiment alive around the stock. Search dominance and AI momentum remain the key narrative.

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy ETF
movers.note: Edged down slightly today to $8.80. Oil dropped sharply last night (nearly 3% to $93.78 USD) after OPEC cut its demand growth forecast for 2026, and India also slashed its fuel demand projections by 40%. That's a headwind for energy stocks.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Tiny gain to $92.51 today — the only ASX holding to close in the green. Emerging markets getting a small lift from a slightly firmer Aussie dollar.

movers.name: Commonwealth Bank
movers.note: Barely moved, closing at $164.30. RBA rate chatter continues — some experts are calling for hikes, others say cuts are coming — but CBA is holding steady for now.

markets.summary: Last night on Wall St was quietly positive — the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both gained, driven by tech optimism. Oil took a decent hit (-3%) after OPEC trimmed its demand outlook. Gold dipped slightly. The Aussie dollar is steady just above 71.6 US cents. Today's ASX 200 close data wasn't available in the feed.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's close — solid gain, tech leading the way.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night's close — best of the main indices, AI/tech stocks in favour.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Today's close data unavailable — previous close was 8,692.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Dropped nearly 3% last night — OPEC cut its 2026 demand forecast and India slashed fuel projections by 40%.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Slight dip — risk appetite improved a little, so gold eased back.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar holding firm around 71.7 cents despite mixed RBA rate signals.

politics.summary: Labor's tax reform agenda is dominating Canberra today — CGT changes, a new $1,000 worker deduction, and RBA rate expectations are all in the mix. It's a busy week for anyone who owns property, earns a salary, or just wants to know what the government is up to.

stories.title: Labor pushes ahead with CGT changes despite calls to pause
stories.why_it_matters: Labor is ignoring industry calls to pause its proposed changes to the capital gains tax (CGT) discount — the tax break you get when selling an asset like an investment property. Currently investors pay tax on only 50% of their capital gain; Labor wants to reduce that discount. This directly affects anyone holding investment properties or shares outside super. The government is pressing ahead despite pushback from the business community.

stories.title: $1,000 worker deduction tied to tax hikes — former Treasury official warns of 'disastrous' Budget move
stories.why_it_matters: The government is proposing a $1,000 tax deduction for workers — but it's being funded by raising taxes elsewhere, including on investors and businesses. A former Treasury official has warned the package could be 'disastrous' for the economy, arguing the trade-off between worker benefits and investment disincentives is badly calibrated. If you're an investor or small business owner, this budget package is worth watching closely.

stories.title: Labor to consult all businesses on tax reform amid criticism
stories.why_it_matters: After significant criticism from the business community over the tax reform agenda, Labor has agreed to consult with all businesses — not just large ones — before finalising changes. This is a slight softening of approach, but the government has made clear the overall direction of reform isn't changing. Worth watching for how this affects small business sentiment over coming weeks.

stories.title: Expert defies consensus and demands RBA hikes rates
stories.why_it_matters: While most economists expect the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to hold or even cut interest rates, at least one prominent expert is bucking that view and calling for more rate hikes. This matters because rate movements affect your mortgage repayments, CBA's lending margins, and the broader equity market. Upcoming Australian inflation data this week could shift the dial — if inflation comes in hot, rate hike bets will rise sharply.

ai.summary: Today's big AI story is Google launching 'Gemini Omni', a new all-in-one model. Meanwhile, Pope Leo XIV has made AI regulation the focus of his first major teaching document — an unusual but significant global voice entering the debate. Europe is also ramping up its approach to AI rules.

stories.title: Google launches Gemini Omni — a new all-in-one AI model
stories.why_it_matters: Google has announced Gemini Omni, described as an all-in-one AI model — meaning it can handle text, images, audio, and video in a single system rather than needing separate tools for each. This is directly relevant to your GOOGL holding: it keeps Google competitive with OpenAI and Microsoft in the AI race. The 'omni' (meaning all-capable) approach is becoming the new battleground, and Google launching one is a positive signal for the stock.

stories.title: Pope Leo XIV calls for AI regulation to 'safeguard humanity' in first major teaching
stories.why_it_matters: Pope Leo XIV has issued what the AFR is calling his first major 'encyclical' (an official teaching document sent to the whole Catholic Church) — and it's about AI, not religion. He's calling for global regulation of AI to protect human dignity and 'safeguard humanity'. With over a billion Catholics worldwide and significant moral authority in many governments, this adds a major new voice to the AI regulation debate — particularly in Europe and Latin America where the Church still holds significant political sway.

stories.title: Germany urges Europe to take 'offensive' approach on AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Germany is pushing the EU to take an 'offensive' rather than defensive stance on AI regulation — meaning proactively shaping global AI rules rather than just reacting to what US and Chinese tech companies do. This is significant for global tech companies like Google and Microsoft that operate in Europe, as tighter or smarter regulation could either constrain their business models or, if done well, create a more level playing field.

stories.title: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini give different answers on which jobs AI will replace
stories.why_it_matters: Researchers asked three major AI chatbots — ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini — which jobs are most at risk from AI. Each gave a different answer, which is interesting in itself: it shows these tools don't have a unified view of the future. Generally, routine white-collar roles (data entry, basic coding, customer service) ranked highly across all three, while hands-on trades and creative roles varied. Worth knowing if you or your family are thinking about career or study choices.
